subject: ss-surgical-gastroenterology
title: Surgical Gastroenterology
curriculum: NMC Competency-Based MCh Surgical Gastroenterology Curriculum / NBEMS NEET-SS Surgical Specialty Group (Surgical Gastroenterology)
examPattern: NEET-SS Surgical Group paper (150 MCQs, 40 percent feeder MS General Surgery and 60 percent super-speciality). Within the super-speciality share, GI surgery and surgical oncology carry 12 to 16 questions: luminal GI and HPB operative decision-making, oncology resections with nodal harvests and margins, emergency HPB and GI surgery, and transplant basics. Weight follows MCh GI surgery university papers (basic sciences, principles, recent advances), the INI-SS important-topic list and the exam-pyq overlays.
book: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd Edition 2025 (Elsevier) for luminal gastrointestinal surgery; Blumgart Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas 6th Edition (Elsevier) for HPB surgery

sections.name: Oesophagus, Stomach, Bariatric Surgery and Upper GI Emergencies

modules.name: Surgical Anatomy, Physiology and Motility Workup of the Oesophagus

mustKnow.fact: The oesophagus has cervical, thoracic and abdominal segments with segmental blood supply, so operative mobilisation must preserve the segmental vessels and the anterior left vagus and posterior right vagus trunks.
The lower oesophageal sphincter is a 3 to 4 cm high-pressure zone reinforced by the crural diaphragm, and a resting pressure below 10 mmHg marks an incompetent barrier that predisposes to reflux.

Chicago Classification version 4 stages motility disorders on high-resolution manometry into achalasia types I to III and oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction using the integrated relaxation pressure.
Ambulatory 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring confirms reflux when the DeMeester score exceeds 14.7 or total acid exposure time exceeds 6 percent, per the Lyon Consensus 2.0.
Timed barium swallow shows a bird-beak tapering in achalasia and a corkscrew rosary-bead pattern in distal oesophageal spasm, with a retained column at 1 and 5 minutes marking poor emptying.

Endoscopic ultrasound stages oesophageal cancer by wall layer for T category and samples celiac nodes by fine-needle aspiration, deciding between endoscopic resection, neoadjuvant therapy and surgery.
Mackler triad of vomiting, chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema with Hamman mediastinal crunch signals oesophageal perforation, confirmed first with water-soluble contrast swallow.

Truncal vagotomy divides both vagal trunks at the diaphragmatic hiatus and always needs a drainage procedure such as pyloroplasty or gastrojejunostomy because denervation abolishes antral pump function.

topics.title: Surgical Anatomy, Physiology and Motility Workup of the Oesophagus

modules.name: GERD, Barrett Oesophagus and Antireflux Surgery

mustKnow.fact: Laparoscopic fundoplication is offered for proven gastroesophageal reflux with large hiatus hernia, refractory oesophagitis or regurgitation, and Nissen 360-degree wrap suits normal motility while Toupet 270-degree posterior wrap suits weak peristalsis.
Barrett oesophagus needs intestinal metaplasia on biopsy with at least 1 cm of columnar lining, and dysplasia grade decides surveillance against endoscopic eradication.

Nondysplastic Barrett undergoes surveillance endoscopy every 3 to 5 years, low-grade dysplasia every 6 to 12 months, and high-grade dysplasia gets radiofrequency ablation with endoscopic mucosal resection of nodules.
Magnetic sphincter augmentation with the LINX device suits small hernias with normal motility but is avoided with large hiatus hernia, severe oesophagitis or nickel allergy.
Failed fundoplication presents with recurrent reflux, dysphagia or gas-bloat, and redo surgery needs manometry and pH-impedance to separate wrap failure from wrong initial indication.
Paraesophageal hernia with gastric volvulus causing Borchardt triad of pain, retching without vomiting and inability to pass a nasogastric tube is a surgical emergency needing urgent reduction.
Short oesophagus recognised when 2 to 3 cm of intra-abdominal oesophagus cannot be achieved without tension needs a Collis gastroplasty lengthening procedure with the fundoplication.
Mesh cruroplasty is reserved for large hiatal defects over 5 cm or redo repairs, using biologic or absorbable mesh because permanent synthetic mesh at the hiatus risks erosion into the oesophagus.

topics.title: GERD, Barrett Oesophagus and Antireflux Surgery

modules.name: Achalasia and Spastic Motility Disorders: Myotomy, POEM and Pneumatic Dilation

mustKnow.fact: Achalasia shows absent peristalsis with impaired lower sphincter relaxation on manometry, and Chicago type II with panesophageal pressurisation responds best to myotomy while type III spastic disease needs extended myotomy.
Laparoscopic Heller myotomy divides circular muscle 6 cm up the oesophagus and 3 cm onto the stomach, always paired with a Dor anterior fundoplication to limit postoperative reflux.
Peroral endoscopic myotomy matches Heller for symptom relief with more reflux, so it suits type III achalasia, sigmoid oesophagus and redo cases where laparoscopy is hostile.
Pneumatic dilation with a 30 to 40 mm Rigiflex balloon tears sphincter fibres and suits older or unfit patients, but perforation in 2 to 4 percent needs immediate surgical backup.
Diffuse oesophageal spasm shows simultaneous contractions over 20 percent of swallows with normal relaxation, and long myotomy or POEM relieves dysphagia when drugs fail.
End-stage achalasia with megaoesophagus over 6 cm diameter, sigmoid tortuosity and failed myotomies needs oesophagectomy with gastric conduit reconstruction.
Pseudoachalasia from cardia tumours is suspected with rapid weight loss under 6 months in patients over 55 years, confirmed by endoscopy with biopsy and cross-sectional imaging.
Botulinum toxin injection into the sphincter gives only months of relief in the frail elderly, and repeated injections scar the plane and complicate later myotomy.

modules.name: Oesophageal Perforation, Caustic Injury and Conduit Reconstruction

mustKnow.fact: Boerhaave spontaneous rupture follows forceful vomiting against a closed glottis, classically tearing the left posterolateral distal oesophagus with mediastinal soilage and sepsis.
The Pittsburgh severity score grades perforation by pleural effusion, fever, leukocytosis and hypotension, with scores above 5 predicting need for surgery over conservative care.

Perforations detected within 24 hours with contained leak and no sepsis suit nil by mouth, broad-spectrum antibiotics, proton pump inhibition and endoscopic stenting, while delayed septic cases need thoracotomy and repair.
Primary repair buttresses the mucosal closure with a pleural, intercostal muscle or pericardial fat flap, and defects over 50 percent of circumference need resection with reconstruction.

Caustic alkali causes liquefactive necrosis with deep injury while acid causes coagulative eschar, graded by Zargar 0 to IIIB on endoscopy done within 24 to 48 hours avoiding the 5 to 15 day sloughing window.

Grade IIIB caustic injury with full-thickness necrosis, mediastinitis or peritonitis needs emergency oesophagectomy with cervical oesophagostomy and feeding jejunostomy, delaying reconstruction by 6 months.
Caustic strictures appearing after 3 to 8 weeks undergo serial endoscopic dilation first, and refractory or long strictures need colonic interposition using left colon on the middle colic pedicle.

The stomach is the first-choice oesophageal conduit on the right gastroepiploic arcade, with colon second and jejunum for short defects, and the anastomosis sits in the neck after McKeown or in the chest after Ivor Lewis resection.

modules.name: Oesophageal and Junctional Cancer: Staging, Neoadjuvant Therapy and Resection

mustKnow.fact: Squamous carcinoma dominates the upper and middle thirds with smoking and alcohol risk, while adenocarcinoma rises from Barrett in the lower third and junction with obesity and reflux risk.
Siewert types I to III locate junctional tumours by epicentre relative to the gastric cardia, deciding between oesophagectomy and extended total gastrectomy.
Locally advanced adenocarcinoma gets CROSS chemoradiotherapy with carboplatin, paclitaxel and 41.4 Gy or perioperative FLOT, then restaging before resection.

Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy pairs abdominal and right thoracic phases with an intrathoracic anastomosis, McKeown adds a cervical anastomosis, and transhiatal avoids thoracotomy in frail patients at the cost of mediastinal blind dissection.
A minimum of 15 lymph nodes in the resection specimen stages oesophageal cancer accurately, and R0 margin with 5 cm proximal clearance is the operative goal.

Anastomotic leak presents on days 5 to 7 with tachycardia, sepsis and neck crepitus or chest soilage, managed by drainage, antibiotics, endoscopic vacuum or stent for contained leaks and reoperation for conduit necrosis.

Chyle leak over 1000 mL per day, jejunal feeding intolerance and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness are screened routinely after oesophagectomy, with thoracic duct ligation for high-output chylothorax.
Definitive chemoradiotherapy suits cervical oesophageal cancer and unfit patients, while salvage oesophagectomy is reserved for residual or recurrent disease after full-dose radiation.

modules.name: Complicated Peptic Ulcer: Bleeding, Perforation and Obstruction

mustKnow.fact: Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs cause most duodenal and gastric ulcers, and eradication with bismuth quadruple or clarithromycin triple therapy for 14 days prevents recurrence and rebleeding.

Forrest Ia spurting and Ib oozing ulcers carry the highest rebleed risk and need combination endoscopic therapy with clips plus thermal coagulation followed by high-dose intravenous proton pump infusion.

Failed endoscopic control of ulcer bleeding goes to catheter embolisation of the gastroduodenal artery first, with oversewing plus truncal vagotomy and pyloroplasty reserved for unstable or recurrent bleeders.
Perforated duodenal ulcer under 1 cm with presentation inside 24 hours and no prior ulcer history suits laparoscopic Graham omental patch repair with lavage and postoperative eradication.
Giant ulcers over 2 cm, malignant-looking or recurrent perforations need distal gastrectomy with Billroth II or Roux-en-Y reconstruction rather than patching.

Gastric outlet obstruction from chronic ulcer disease shows succussion splash, hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and needs 2 to 4 weeks of nasogastric decompression and acid suppression before gastrojejunostomy.
Type I gastric ulcers sit on the lesser curvature with normal acid, type II combine gastric with duodenal ulcer and high acid, and type III prepyloric ulcers behave like duodenal disease.
Every gastric ulcer needs multiple edge biopsies to exclude cancer, with repeat endoscopy at 8 to 12 weeks proving healing, because 5 percent of benign-looking ulcers harbour malignancy.

modules.name: Gastric Cancer: D2 Gastrectomy, GIST and Gastric Lymphoma

mustKnow.fact: Intestinal-type distal cancers link to Helicobacter, smoking and salted foods while diffuse linitis plastica with signet rings links to CDH1 germline mutation needing prophylactic total gastrectomy.
Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal cytology precedes curative surgery for T3, T4 or node-positive disease because positive cytology upstages to metastatic M1 disease.

Distal tumours get subtotal gastrectomy with 5 cm proximal margin, proximal and junctional tumours get total gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y oesophagojejunostomy, and D2 nodal dissection harvests at least 16 nodes.
Perioperative FLOT chemotherapy improves survival in resectable T2 or higher disease, and adjuvant S-1 or capecitabine with oxaliplatin follows D2 resection in Asian protocols.
Gastric GIST under 2 cm without high-risk features suits wedge resection with 1 to 2 cm margins avoiding lymphadenectomy, since nodal spread is rare.

KIT exon 11 mutation predicts imatinib response, high-risk GIST over 5 cm or over 5 mitoses per 5 square mm gets 3 years of adjuvant imatinib 400 mg daily, and PDGFRA D842V resists imatinib but responds to avapritinib.
Gastric MALT lymphoma with Helicobacter positivity regresses with eradication alone in 80 percent, while deep invasion or t(11;18) translocation needs radiotherapy or rituximab-based therapy.

Krükenberg ovarian metastases, Sister Mary Joseph umbilical nodule and Blumer shelf on rectal examination mark transcoelomic spread where surgery is palliative with bypass or stenting for obstruction.

modules.name: Bariatric and Metabolic Surgery: Sleeve, Bypass and Complications

mustKnow.fact: Metabolic surgery is offered at body mass index over 40, or over 35 with comorbidity, and over 30 with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes after failed medical therapy, following multidisciplinary assessment.
Sleeve gastrectomy removes 75 to 80 percent of stomach over a 36 to 40 French bougie, preserving pylorus with lower ulcer risk but worsening reflux in 20 percent.

Roux-en-Y gastric bypass builds a 30 mL pouch with 75 to 150 cm alimentary and 50 cm biliopancreatic limbs, giving superior diabetes remission and reflux control at the cost of internal hernia and ulcer risk.
One-anastomosis gastric bypass uses a 200 cm biliopancreatic limb with single gastrojejunostomy, effective for weight and diabetes but with bile reflux and malabsorption needing surveillance.
Early leak within 7 days shows tachycardia over 120, fever and shoulder pain and needs urgent washout with drainage, while late strictures at 3 to 6 weeks respond to endoscopic dilation.
Petersen defect between mesenteries and the jejunojejunal mesenteric defect must both be closed with nonabsorbable suture at bypass surgery, since internal hernia peaks after major weight loss.

Lifelong multivitamins with calcium, vitamin D, B12, iron and thiamine follow all bariatric procedures, with copper and zinc after bypass, because deficiencies cause anaemia, neuropathy and Wernicke disease.

Dumping with vasomotor flushing 30 minutes after sugars and late hypoglycaemia at 1 to 3 hours follows bypass and sleeve, managed by small low-glycaemic meals with separated fluids before revision surgery.

sections.name: Small Bowel, Appendix, Colorectal and Anorectal Surgery

modules.name: Small Bowel Obstruction: Adhesions, Workup and Operative Timing

mustKnow.fact: Postoperative adhesions cause 70 percent of small bowel obstructions, and a virgin abdomen with obstruction points to hernia, malignancy, Crohn disease or gallstone ileus instead.
Contrast CT with oral Gastrografin distinguishes partial from complete obstruction, and contrast reaching the colon within 24 hours predicts nonoperative resolution with 95 percent accuracy.
Peritonitis, strangulation with closed-loop beaking, pneumatosis with portal venous gas, and deterioration after 48 to 72 hours of conservative care mandate laparotomy.
Rigler triad of small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia and ectopic gallstone marks gallstone ileus impacting at the ileocecal valve, treated by enterolithotomy alone in the acute setting.
Internal hernias through Petersen, paraduodenal or foramen of Winslow defects trap dilated loops with mesenteric swirl on CT and need urgent reduction with defect closure.
Intussusception in adults is pathological with a lead point such as polyp, Meckel diverticulum or tumour in 90 percent, so resection without reduction is the rule for colonic cases.
Meckel diverticulum follows the rule of twos at 2 percent prevalence, 2 feet from the valve and 2 inches long, bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa detected by technetium-99m Meckel scan.
Laparoscopic adhesiolysis suits first-episode partial obstruction with mild distension under 4 cm, while massive distension, dense midline scarring or strangulation needs open surgery.

modules.name: Crohn Disease Surgery: Strictures, Fistulae and Perianal Disease

mustKnow.fact: Surgery is indicated for fibrostenotic stricture, fistulising disease, abscess, toxic megacolon and growth failure, while active luminal inflammation without complications stays medical.
Short strictures under 10 cm in quiescent bowel get Heineke-Mikulicz stricturoplasty and longer ones get Finney or side-to-side isoperistaltic stricturoplasty to preserve bowel length.
Ileocolic resection removes the diseased segment with primary anastomosis, and Kono-S antimesenteric functional end-to-end anastomosis lowers surgical recurrence.
Perianal Crohn with complex fistulae needs examination under anaesthesia with seton drainage plus anti-TNF therapy, and proctectomy is reserved for destroyed incontinent rectums.
Enterovesical fistula shows pneumaturia and recurrent urinary infections, confirmed by CT with oral contrast, and needs resection of the bowel segment with bladder cuff repair.
Toxic megacolon with transverse colon over 6 cm plus systemic toxicity needs urgent subtotal colectomy with ileostomy, avoiding primary anastomosis in the emergency setting.
Smoking doubles postoperative Crohn recurrence, so cessation, 6-month colonoscopic Rutgeerts scoring and timely prophylaxis with thiopurines or anti-TNF protect the anastomosis.
Intra-abdominal abscess over 3 cm gets percutaneous drainage with antibiotics first, and resection follows after 6 to 8 weeks once sepsis resolves and nutrition is rebuilt.

modules.name: Ulcerative Colitis Surgery: Colectomy, IPAA Pouch and Pouchitis

mustKnow.fact: Acute severe colitis needs rescue infliximab or ciclosporin on day 3 by Travis criteria, and colectomy on days 4 to 7 if stool frequency, CRP and albumin fail to improve.
Restorative proctocolectomy with J-pouch ileal pouch-anal anastomosis is the standard for fit young patients, staged as subtotal colectomy first in emergency or steroid-loaded cases.
Pouchitis with urgency, bleeding and fever responds to 2 weeks of ciprofloxacin with metronidazole, and chronic antibiotic-dependent cases step up to probiotics or biologics.
Dysplasia in flat mucosa or strictures in longstanding pancolitis over 8 years mandates proctocolectomy because surveillance misses synchronous cancer.
Ileorectal anastomosis preserves fertility and avoids pelvic dissection but leaves rectal cancer risk needing lifelong surveillance, suiting older or poor-sphincter patients.
Continent Brooke ileostomy with Kock pouch suits failed pouches and poor sphincters, using a nipple valve that needs intubation 4 to 6 times daily.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis with ulcerative colitis raises colorectal cancer and cholangiocarcinoma risk, mandating annual colonoscopy with chromoendoscopy from diagnosis.
Laparoscopic colectomy matches open surgery for cancer clearance with faster recovery, but toxic megacolon with caecal diameter over 9 cm needs urgent open subtotal colectomy.

modules.name: Appendicitis, Interval Surgery and Appendiceal Neoplasms

mustKnow.fact: Alvarado score combines migratory pain, anorexia, nausea, right iliac fossa tenderness, rebound, fever, leukocytosis and neutrophilia, with 7 or more predicting appendicitis needing surgery.
Uncomplicated appendicitis gets laparoscopic appendectomy within 24 hours, while antibiotics-first suits selected cases but carries 30 percent one-year recurrence.
Complicated appendicitis with phlegmon or abscess over 3 cm gets percutaneous drainage with interval appendectomy at 6 to 8 weeks because immediate surgery risks bowel injury.
Appendicolith with nonperforated appendicitis raises failure of antibiotics alone to 40 percent, favouring early appendectomy in faecolith cases.
Carcinoid under 1 cm at the tip needs appendectomy alone, 1 to 2 cm tumours need right hemicolectomy with mesoappendiceal invasion, and over 2 cm always needs colectomy.
Low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm with pseudomyxoma peritonei needs cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC at a peritoneal centre, not appendectomy alone.
Stump appendicitis months after appendectomy shows a residual stump over 5 mm on CT and needs completion appendectomy with stump inversion.
Pregnancy shifts the appendix upward after the first trimester, so graded-compression ultrasound first and MRI second avoid ionising radiation, with laparoscopy safe in all trimesters.

modules.name: Colorectal Cancer Surgery: TME, CME, Margins and Obstruction

mustKnow.fact: Total mesorectal excision in the holy plane with 2 cm distal margin and 1 mm circumferential margin is the rectal cancer standard, preserving autonomic nerves for urinary and sexual function.
Complete mesocolic excision with central vascular ligation harvests at least 12 nodes for colon cancer staging, and apical node positivity upstages prognosis.

Mid and low rectal cancers get long-course chemoradiotherapy 50.4 Gy or short-course 25 Gy in 5 fractions, then total mesorectal excision at 6 to 12 weeks, with watch-and-wait for complete clinical responders.
Obstructing left-sided cancers get self-expanding metallic stents as bridge to elective resection or palliation, while right-sided obstructions go straight to extended right hemicolectomy.

Synchronous liver metastases with asymptomatic primary suit liver-first or simultaneous resection in expert centres, and disappearing metastases after chemotherapy still need resection of the original site.
Hartmann procedure with end colostomy suits perforated diverticular or malignant obstruction with faecal peritonitis and unstable patients, reversed after 3 to 6 months.
Defunctioning loop ileostomy protects low anastomoses within 5 cm of the anal verge, and is reversed at 8 to 12 weeks after water-soluble contrast enema confirms healing.
Lynch screening with microsatellite instability or mismatch repair testing on every colorectal cancer guides extended colectomy and family cascade testing for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2 carriers.

modules.name: Hereditary Polyposis and Lynch: Prophylactic Surgery and Surveillance

mustKnow.fact: Familial adenomatous polyposis from APC mutation on chromosome 5q21 shows hundreds of adenomas by teens with 100 percent cancer risk, needing prophylactic colectomy by age 25.
Attenuated FAP with under 100 adenomas and MAP from biallelic MUTYH suit ileorectal anastomosis with rectal surveillance, while dense polyposis needs proctocolectomy with pouch.
Amsterdam II criteria of 3 relatives with Lynch cancers across 2 generations with 1 under 50 years select families for mismatch repair testing.
Lynch colorectal cancer gets extended colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis rather than segmental resection because metachronous cancer risk reaches 30 percent at 10 years.
Peutz-Jeghers STK11 mutation causes hamartomas with mucocutaneous pigmentation and intussusception needing enteroscopic polypectomy, plus breast and pancreatic surveillance.
Juvenile polyposis from SMAD4 or BMPR1A and Cowden PTEN hamartomas need upper and lower surveillance from age 15 because of gastric and colorectal cancer risk.
Desmoid tumours in FAP cluster after prophylactic surgery and are managed with sulindac, anti-oestrogens or sorafenib first, reserving surgery for complications because recurrence is high.

Duodenal adenomatosis needs Spigelman staging with side-viewing endoscopy, and stage IV disease needs pancreas-sparing duodenectomy or Whipple because duodenal cancer is the leading killer after colectomy.

modules.name: Diverticular Disease: Hinchey Staging, Hartmann and Elective Resection

mustKnow.fact: Hinchey stages perforated diverticulitis from pericolic abscess through pelvic, purulent and faecal peritonitis, deciding between antibiotics, drainage, lavage and Hartmann resection.
Uncomplicated diverticulitis without systemic features needs no routine antibiotics, while abscesses 3 to 5 cm get antibiotics and over 5 cm need percutaneous drainage.
Hartmann with end colostomy remains the choice for faecal peritonitis and unstable patients, while stable purulent peritonitis suits primary anastomosis with or without diversion.
Elective sigmoidectomy follows complicated or smouldering diverticulitis, and shared decision-making weighs the 30 percent recurrence against operative risk rather than counting episodes.
Colovesical fistula shows pneumaturia and faecaluria with a saw-tooth bladder on CT, treated by sigmoid resection with bladder curettage, not cystectomy.
Diverticular bleeding stops spontaneously in 80 percent and localises by CT angiography at bleeding rates over 0.3 mL per minute, with embolisation before segmental colectomy.
Giant colonic diverticulum over 4 cm risks perforation and needs segmental resection because barium enema balloon sign can mask coexistent cancer.
Right-sided diverticulitis mimics appendicitis in young patients, and uncomplicated cases resolve with conservative care avoiding unnecessary appendectomy.

modules.name: Benign Anorectal Disease: Piles, Fistula, Fissure and Prolapse

mustKnow.fact: Internal haemorrhoids grade by prolapse from I with bleeding only to IV with irreducible prolapse, and grades I to II get band ligation while III to IV need stapled haemorrhoidopexy or excisional haemorrhoidectomy.

Parks classification maps fistula tracts as intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric and extrasphincteric, and Goodsall rule predicts a curved posterior tract from a midline posterior opening.
Low simple fistulae get fistulotomy laying open the tract, while high complex tracts involving over 30 percent of sphincter need seton, LIFT ligation or advancement flap to preserve continence.
Chronic posterior midline fissure with sentinel pile and hypertrophied papilla failing 6 weeks of diltiazem or nitrates needs lateral internal sphincterotomy to the dentate line.
Pilonidal disease with midline pits and abscess gets drainage first, then Bascom cleft-lift or Karydakis flap off-midline closure because midline wounds recur most.

Full-thickness rectal prolapse over 5 cm in the fit young suits laparoscopic ventral mesh rectopexy preserving nerves, while perineal Delorme or Altemeier suits frail elderly under spinal anaesthesia.
Anal squamous carcinoma under 5 cm gets Nigro chemoradiotherapy with 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin as primary therapy, reserving abdominoperineal resection for salvage.
Hidradenitis suppurativa of the perineum with recurrent boils and sinus tracts needs wide excision with secondary healing or flap cover because antibiotics alone never cure established disease.

modules.name: Mesenteric Ischaemia: Acute Embolic, NOMI, Venous and Chronic

mustKnow.fact: Acute embolic ischaemia from atrial fibrillation lodges at the superior mesenteric artery branch points with pain out of proportion, lactic acidosis and a 50 to 90 percent mortality when revascularisation is delayed.
Biphasic CT angiography is the test of choice showing SMA cutoff, pneumatosis and portal venous gas, and must precede laparotomy to plan embolectomy against bypass.
Nonocclusive mesenteric ischaemia follows low-flow states on vasopressors and improves with resuscitation, prostaglandin infusion and stopping vasoconstrictors rather than surgery.
Mesenteric venous thrombosis with hypercoagulable states or portal hypertension gets therapeutic heparin then 6 months of anticoagulation, with surgery only for infarction or peritonitis.
Second-look laparotomy at 24 to 48 hours reassesses bowel viability after embolectomy, using fluorescein or Doppler to separate viable from gangrenous segments.
Chronic mesenteric ischaemia shows food fear with weight loss and 2 of 3 vessel stenoses, treated by endovascular stenting of the celiac and SMA or open bypass.
Median arcuate ligament syndrome compresses the celiac axis in young thin women with postprandial pain relieved by expiration on duplex, cured by laparoscopic ligament release.
Ischaemic colitis at the watershed Griffith point and Sudeck point presents with bloody diarrhoea within 48 hours of hypotension, and gangrene or stricture needs segmental resection.

modules.name: Liver Anatomy, Volumetry and Resection Techniques

mustKnow.fact: Couinaud divides the liver into 8 functional segments each with portal triad supply, with the Cantlie line through the middle hepatic vein separating right and left hemilivers.
Future liver remnant must exceed 20 percent in normal liver, 30 percent after chemotherapy or steatosis, and 40 percent in cirrhosis, measured by CT volumetry.
Portal vein embolisation of the resected side hypertrophies the remnant in 4 to 6 weeks, and failure to grow predicts post-hepatectomy liver failure.
ALPPS partitions the liver with portal ligation for rapid 7 to 14 day hypertrophy in staged resection, reserved for tiny remnants because of higher morbidity.
Pringle inflow occlusion in 15-minute clamp and 5-minute release cycles limits blood loss, and periods beyond 60 minutes risk ischaemic injury to the remnant.
Anterior approach with hanging manoeuvre avoids tumour rupture in large right-lobe lesions, and selective hemihepatic vascular exclusion preserves remnant perfusion.
Post-hepatectomy bile leak over 50 mL per day beyond postoperative day 3 is ISGLS grade B or C and needs ERCP stenting or percutaneous drainage.
Laparoscopic major hepatectomy matches open resection for benign disease and colorectal metastases in expert centres, with Louisville criteria guiding case selection.

modules.name: Liver Trauma: AAST Grading, Nonoperative Care and Packing

mustKnow.fact: AAST grades liver injury I to VI from subcapsular haematoma under 10 percent surface to hepatic avulsion, with grade III over 3 cm parenchymal depth marking major injury.
Haemodynamically stable blunt injury without peritonitis gets nonoperative management with bed rest, serial haemoglobin and CT follow-up, succeeding in over 85 percent.
Contrast blush with instability goes to immediate laparotomy, while blush in a stable patient without peritonitis goes to angioembolisation with rescanning.
Perihepatic packing with laparotomy pads controls major bleeding in damage control surgery, with relook and pack removal at 24 to 48 hours.
Juxtahepatic venous injury with retrohepatic caval bleeding needs atriocaval shunting or total vascular exclusion, carrying mortality over 50 percent.
Delayed haemobilia with melena and right upper quadrant pain days after trauma comes from arteriobiliary fistula and is diagnosed and treated by hepatic angiography with embolisation.
Bile leak and biloma after trauma get ERCP sphincterotomy with stenting to lower ductal pressure, and major ductal disruption needs hepaticojejunostomy.
Penetrating injury with peritonitis or evisceration goes straight to laparotomy, and tractotomy with selective vessel ligation beats formal lobectomy for through-and-through wounds.

modules.name: Hydatid Disease of the Liver: PAIR, Surgery and Albendazole

mustKnow.fact: Echinococcus granulosus from dog faeces forms unilocular liver cysts in 70 percent of hydatid cases, with right lobe predominance and slow growth of 1 cm per year.
WHO stages CE1 to CE5 separate active unilocular and multivesicular cysts from transitional degenerating and inactive calcified cysts, deciding between drugs, PAIR and surgery.
PAIR puncture-aspiration-injection-reaspiration suits CE1 and CE3a cysts over 5 cm, using hypertonic saline or alcohol scolicidal with albendazole cover.
Albendazole 400 mg twice daily in 28-day cycles with 14-day breaks, or continuously with monitoring, sterilises small cysts and must precede and follow any intervention.
Cystobiliary communication with jaundice, cholangitis or hydatid membranes in bile needs ERCP clearance plus surgery with cavity-bile leak closure and omentoplasty.
Pericystectomy removes the cyst with its fibrous capsule for peripheral lesions, while central cysts near vessels get partial pericystectomy with capitonnage to avoid major bleeding.
Intraoperative spillage risks anaphylaxis and secondary peritoneal hydatidosis, prevented by scolicidal-soaked packs, closed aspiration and albendazole prophylaxis.
Alveolar echinococcosis from Echinococcus multilocularis behaves like cancer with infiltrative growth, needing radical resection with 2 cm margins plus 2 years of albendazole.

modules.name: Liver Abscess: Pyogenic, Amoebic and Drainage Decisions

mustKnow.fact: Pyogenic abscess from biliary sepsis, portal pyaemia or Klebsiella hypervirulent strains shows fever with right upper pain, leukocytosis and rim-enhancing lesions on contrast CT.
Amoebic abscess from Entamoeba histolytica gives anchovy-sauce aspirate with negative bacterial culture and positive serology, resolving with metronidazole 750 mg thrice daily for 7 to 10 days.
Abscesses over 5 cm, left-lobe location threatening rupture, or failed 48-hour antibiotic trial need percutaneous pigtail drainage with 8 to 12 French catheters.
Ruptured amoebic abscess into peritoneum or thorax needs urgent drainage with washout plus metronidazole, while contained leaks respond to catheter drainage alone.
Klebsiella liver abscess with endophthalmitis or meningitis marks metastatic hypervirulent K1 disease needing dilated eye examination and prolonged ceftriaxone.
Multiple small miliary abscesses under 3 cm from ascending cholangitis resolve with biliary stenting plus antibiotics, and surgery is reserved for the underlying biliary stricture.
Caudate lobe abscess abutting the vena cava is drained percutaneously under CT guidance rather than surgically because open access risks caval injury.
Follow-up ultrasound at 2 weeks confirms cavity collapse, and persistent thick-walled cavities beyond 6 weeks need re-aspiration with tuberculosis and fungal cultures.

modules.name: Hepatocellular Carcinoma: BCLC, Resection, Transplant and Ablation

mustKnow.fact: Barcelona Clinic stages 0 and A with a single tumour of any size or 3 nodules under 3 cm suit resection or ablation, while portal vein tumour thrombus marks stage C needing systemic therapy.
Alpha-fetoprotein over 400 ng per mL with arterial hyperenhancement plus portal washout on multiphasic CT diagnoses HCC without biopsy in cirrhosis.
Milan single tumour up to 5 cm or 3 nodules up to 3 cm without vascular invasion selects transplant candidates with 4-year survival over 70 percent.
Radiofrequency ablation cures tumours under 3 cm with 1 cm ablative margins, while microwave ablation suits perivascular lesions because of less heat-sink effect.
Transarterial chemoembolisation with doxorubicin-lipiodol suits intermediate multinodular disease without vascular invasion, repeated on demand by mRECIST response.
Atezolizumab with bevacizumab is first-line systemic therapy for advanced HCC with Child-Pugh A liver function after variceal screening, beating sorafenib in the IMBRAVE150 trial.
Fibrolamellar HCC in young noncirrhotic livers shows a central scar with calcification, and aggressive resection with nodal clearance gives 5-year survival near 70 percent.
Ruptured HCC with haemoperitoneum needs transarterial embolisation first for haemostasis, then staged hepatectomy after 4 to 6 weeks once the patient stabilises.

modules.name: Colorectal Liver Metastases: Resectability, Two-Stage and Parenchymal Sparing

mustKnow.fact: Resectability needs R0 clearance with adequate remnant and no unresectable extrahepatic disease, and bilobar or large lesions are converted by chemotherapy rather than judged by number alone.
Fong clinical risk scores node-positive primary, disease-free interval under 12 months, over 1 metastasis, largest over 5 cm and CEA over 200, with higher scores predicting recurrence.
Two-stage hepatectomy clears one lobe first with portal vein embolisation, then the second lobe after 4 to 6 weeks of hypertrophy, suiting bilobar disease with small remnant.
Parenchymal-sparing nonanatomical resections with 1 mm margins preserve remnant for repeat hepatectomy, and wider margins add no survival over R0.
Disappearing metastases after chemotherapy still harbour viable tumour in 80 percent of sites, so the original liver sites must be resected or ablated.
Simultaneous colon and liver resection suits minor hepatectomy with uncomplicated primary, while major hepatectomy or obstructed primaries need staged surgery.
Radiofrequency ablation with 1 cm margins treats deep lesions under 3 cm sparing parenchyma, combined with resection for bilobar disease in one sitting.
Hepatic arterial infusion with floxuridine through an implantable pump controls liver-only disease after resection in high-risk patients at specialised centres.

modules.name: Benign Liver Lesions: Haemangioma, FNH, Adenoma and Cysts

mustKnow.fact: Cavernous haemangioma shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in on contrast CT, and giant lesions over 10 cm or Kasabach-Merritt coagulopathy need enucleation.
Focal nodular hyperplasia shows a central scar with radiating septa and normal liver function, managed by observation with biopsy only when adenoma cannot be excluded.
Hepatocellular adenoma over 5 cm, beta-catenin mutated subtype or male sex needs resection because of bleeding and malignant transformation risk, and oral contraceptives must stop.
Simple liver cysts with thin walls and no enhancement are observed, while symptomatic dominant cysts over 10 cm get laparoscopic fenestration with omental packing.
Polycystic liver disease with Gigot type II dominant cysts suits fenestration, while diffuse type III with intractable symptoms needs transplantation evaluation.
Biliary hamartomas under 5 mm as von Meyenburg complexes are incidental and need no follow-up, unlike mucinous cystic neoplasms with septations that need complete resection.
Pyogenic granuloma-like peliosis from steroids or Bartonella shows blood-filled cavities and reverses on withdrawing the drug, distinguished from adenoma by reticulin preservation.
Hepatic angiomyolipoma with fat density and HMB-45 positivity is observed when small, and resection is reserved for diagnostic doubt or growth over 5 cm.

modules.name: Portal Hypertension: Variceal Bleed, TIPS, Shunts and Devascularisation

mustKnow.fact: Hepatic venous pressure gradient over 10 mmHg marks clinically significant portal hypertension and over 12 mmHg predicts variceal bleeding, measured by transjugular catheterisation.
Acute variceal bleed gets vasoactive octreotide or terlipressin plus antibiotics and band ligation within 12 hours, with balloon tamponade as bridge for refractory bleeding.
Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours suits Child-Pugh B with active bleeding or Child-Pugh C under 14 points, cutting rebleeding and mortality.
Secondary prophylaxis combines nonselective beta-blockers titrated to heart rate 55 to 60 with repeat banding every 2 to 4 weeks until eradication.
Distal splenorenal Warren shunt decompresses varices while preserving portal flow to the liver, suiting Child-Pugh A patients with refractory bleeding and good hepatic reserve.
Portocaval side-to-side shunt fully diverts portal flow with high encephalopathy risk, now reserved for transplant-ineligible Child-Pugh A patients with failed TIPS.
Sugiura devascularisation with oesophageal transection and splenectomy suits noncirrhotic portal fibrosis and extrahepatic portal vein obstruction where shunts fail.
Gastric fundal varices with red signs get cyanoacrylate glue injection, and balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration suits gastrorenal shunts when TIPS is contraindicated.

modules.name: Liver Transplantation: Indications, Technique and Complications

mustKnow.fact: King College criteria list paracetamol acidosis with pH under 7.3, INR over 6.5 with encephalopathy, and creatinine over 300 micromol per L as triggers for super-urgent listing in acute liver failure.
Model for End-Stage Liver Disease over 15 prioritises transplant listing, with exception points for HCC within Milan and for portopulmonary or hepatopulmonary syndromes.
Piggyback caval preservation avoids venovenous bypass and keeps haemodynamics stable, while the duct-to-duct biliary anastomosis over a T-tube suits intact recipient ducts.
Hepatic artery thrombosis within 2 weeks shows rising transaminases with absent Doppler flow and needs urgent revascularisation or retransplantation to prevent graft loss.
Acute cellular rejection with fever, graft tenderness and transaminitis in weeks 2 to 6 responds to pulse methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days.
Tacrolimus troughs of 8 to 12 ng per mL early and 5 to 8 later balance rejection against nephrotoxicity, with mycophenolate and steroids tapered by 3 months.
Living-donor right-lobe grafts need graft-to-recipient weight ratio over 0.8 percent and remnant over 30 percent in the donor, with middle hepatic vein decision by volumetry.
Biliary strictures months after transplant get ERCP dilation with stenting first, and recurrent cholangitis with diffuse ischaemic cholangiopathy needs retransplant evaluation.

modules.name: Gallstones, Cholecystitis and CBD Stones: Timing and Approach

mustKnow.fact: Asymptomatic gallstones need no treatment with under 2 percent yearly biliary pain risk, while biliary colic with wall thickening over 3 mm and Murphy sign marks acute cholecystitis.
Tokyo grades cholecystitis as mild localised, moderate with palpable mass or symptom duration over 72 hours, and severe with organ dysfunction, deciding between early surgery and drainage.

Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of cholecystitis onset beats delayed surgery for complications and stay, with critical view of safety exposing two structures entering the gallbladder.

Common bile duct stones with cholangitis, jaundice or dilated duct over 6 mm need preoperative ERCP clearance, while single-stage laparoscopic bile duct exploration suits fit patients with large stones.
Mirizzi syndrome compresses the common hepatic duct from an impacted cystic duct stone, classified Csendes I to V up to cholecystobiliary fistula needing hepaticojejunostomy.
Bouveret syndrome with gastric outlet obstruction from a cholecystoduodenal (biliary-enteric) fistula stone over 2.5 cm needs enterolithotomy first, with cholecystectomy deferred to a second stage.
Gallbladder polyps over 10 mm, sessile morphology or primary sclerosing cholangitis background need cholecystectomy because of malignant potential.
Percutaneous cholecystostomy bridges severe cholecystitis in unfit patients, with interval cholecystectomy at 6 to 8 weeks once sepsis resolves and fitness improves.

modules.name: Bile Duct Injury: Strasberg Grading, Prevention and Repair

mustKnow.fact: Strasberg grades injury A to E from cystic stump leak through lateral injury to transection with loss of confluence, and type E with excised segment length decides the repair level.
Bismuth-Corlette types I to V locate strictures from distal stump over 2 cm to hilar separation, with type V involving an aberrant right sectoral duct, guiding the height of hepaticojejunostomy.
Critical view of safety with two structures, Rouviere sulcus landmark and intraoperative cholangiogram in unclear anatomy prevents most major injuries.
Hepp-Couinaud technique opens the left hepatic duct along the hilar plate for a wide side-to-side hepaticojejunostomy with 60 to 70 cm Roux limb to prevent reflux cholangitis.
Early repair within 72 hours by a hepatobiliary surgeon matches delayed repair results, while sepsis and inflammation favour drainage first with definitive repair at 6 weeks.
Postoperative bile leak with drain bilirubin over 3 times serum on day 3 is ISGLS grade A when self-limiting and grade B or C when needing ERCP stenting or reoperation.
Vascular injury with right hepatic artery damage accompanies 30 percent of major bile duct injuries and needs CT angiography because ischaemia threatens any repair.
Long-term stricture surveillance with liver function and MRCP detects secondary biliary cirrhosis, and redo hepaticojejunostomy suits failed repairs before transplantation.

modules.name: Choledochal Cyst and APBDJ: Excision and Malignancy Risk

mustKnow.fact: Todani types I to V span fusiform extrahepatic dilation, saccular diverticulum, choledochocele, intrahepatic Caroli disease and combined disease, with type I commonest.
Anomalous pancreaticobiliary duct junction with a long common channel over 15 mm lets pancreatic juice reflux into bile, driving cyst formation and gallbladder cancer.
Complete cyst excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy is the standard for types I and IV because retained cyst carries up to 30 percent lifetime cholangiocarcinoma risk.
Type III choledochocele gets endoscopic sphincterotomy rather than excision, while Caroli disease confined to one lobe gets hepatectomy and diffuse disease needs transplantation.
Childhood presentation with the triad of pain, jaundice and a palpable mass is classic but seen in under 20 percent, and most children present with pancreatitis or cholangitis.
Intraoperative cholangiogram and biopsy of suspicious areas detect synchronous cancer in 10 percent of adult cysts, mandating frozen section before reconstruction.
Post-excision surveillance with annual liver function and MRCP detects anastomotic stricture and remnant intrapancreatic cyst malignancy lifelong.
Gallbladder cancer coexists with maljunction without stones, so prophylactic cholecystectomy is advised when the junction is anomalous even without a cyst.

modules.name: Cholangiocarcinoma: Perihilar Klatskin, Staging and Resectability

mustKnow.fact: Perihilar Klatskin tumours at the confluence are typed Bismuth-Corlette I to IV by ductal extent, and type IV with bilateral secondary radical involvement is usually unresectable.
Painless jaundice with pruritus, weight loss and a Courvoisier palpable gallbladder marks malignant distal obstruction needing triple-phase CT plus MRCP for staging.

Resectability needs unilateral vascular preservation with adequate remnant, no bilateral secondary biliary involvement and no distant spread, with staging laparoscopy detecting occult metastases in 25 percent.
Preoperative biliary drainage is reserved for cholangitis, severe malnutrition or planned portal embolisation because routine drainage raises septic complications.
Extended hepatectomy with caudate lobectomy and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy is the curative operation for perihilar disease, harvesting at least 6 nodes.
Liver transplantation with neoadjuvant chemoradiation under Mayo protocol suits unresectable perihilar tumours under 3 cm without metastases, with 5-year survival near 70 percent.
Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma over 5 cm or multifocal gets gemcitabine with cisplatin first, and FGFR2 fusions respond to pemigatinib while IDH1 mutation responds to ivosidenib.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis with dominant stricture and CA 19-9 over 100 units per mL needs brush cytology with FISH polysomy because of 10 to 15 percent lifetime cancer risk.

modules.name: Gallbladder Cancer: Incidental Disease, Staging and Extended Cholecystectomy

mustKnow.fact: Gallstones over 3 cm, porcelain calcification and polyps over 10 mm raise gallbladder cancer risk, endemic in North India with female predominance.
Incidental T1a disease confined to mucosa after simple cholecystectomy needs no further surgery with 5-year survival near 100 percent, while T1b into muscle needs extended resection.
Extended cholecystectomy removes liver segments IVb and V with 2 cm margins plus portal nodal clearance of at least 6 nodes for T1b and T2 disease.
T3 disease breaching serosa and T4 with vascular invasion get neoadjuvant gemcitabine-cisplatin first, with surgery only for responders without distant spread.
Jaundice at presentation usually marks unresectable disease with hilar invasion, and palliation uses endoscopic metal stenting with 8 to 12 month patency.
Port-site recurrence after laparoscopic cholecystectomy for unsuspected cancer adds excision of port sites with the definitive resection specimen.
Adjuvant capecitabine for 6 months after R0 resection improves survival per BILCAP, and surveillance with 3-monthly imaging catches the early recurrence peak.
Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis mimics cancer with wall thickening and infiltration, distinguished by intact mucosa on imaging and frozen section at surgery.

modules.name: Benign Biliary Strictures, PSC and Recurrent Cholangitis

mustKnow.fact: Postoperative strictures present months after cholecystectomy with cholestasis and cholangitis, and MRCP maps the level while endoscopic dilation with multiple plastic stents treats short lesions.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis shows beaded ducts with ulcerative colitis in 70 percent, progressing to cirrhosis with 10 to 15 percent cholangiocarcinoma risk.
Dominant strictures under 1.5 mm in PSC with rising bilirubin need balloon dilation with brush cytology because of cancer risk, repeated annually.
IgG4 sclerosing cholangitis with serum IgG4 over 135 mg per dL and sausage pancreas responds to prednisolone 0.6 mg per kg, distinguished from cancer by steroid trial.
Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis with intrahepatic pigment stones and strictures in Southeast Asia needs hepatectomy for atrophic segments with hepatolithiasis plus biliary access loop.
Biliary parasitic infestation with Ascaris or Clonorchis causes relapsing cholangitis, cleared by ERCP extraction with albendazole, and chronic Clonorchis raises cholangiocarcinoma risk.
Charcot triad of pain, fever and jaundice marks cholangitis while Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion marking suppurative disease needing urgent drainage.
Severe cholangitis with organ dysfunction needs ERCP drainage within 6 hours, moderate disease within 24 hours, and mild disease electively after antibiotics.

modules.name: Acute Pancreatitis: Necrosis, Step-Up and Compartment Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: Revised Atlanta classifies interstitial oedematous against necrotising disease, with organ failure under 48 hours marking moderately severe and persistent failure marking severe pancreatitis.

Gallstones and alcohol cause 80 percent of attacks, with triglycerides over 1000 mg per dL and calcium over 10 mg per dL as metabolic triggers needing same-admission cholecystectomy for biliary cases.
Contrast CT at 72 to 96 hours stages necrosis and detects gas in infected necrosis, while early CT underestimates necrosis and is reserved for diagnostic doubt.

Infected necrosis with gas, positive culture or persistent sepsis beyond 4 weeks follows the PANTER step-up from percutaneous drainage through endoscopic necrosectomy to minimally invasive retroperitoneal debridement.
Walled-off necrosis after 4 weeks with obstruction, pain or infection gets endoscopic cystgastrostomy with lumen-apposing metal stents rather than open surgery.
Abdominal compartment syndrome with bladder pressure over 20 mmHg plus organ failure needs decompressive laparotomy, and percutaneous drainage is tried first when collections dominate.
Enteral feeding within 48 hours through nasojejunal tube preserves gut barrier and cuts infection, while prophylactic antibiotics and probiotics do not prevent infected necrosis.
Cholangitis with biliary pancreatitis needs ERCP within 24 hours, while mere biliary obstruction without cholangitis waits for the attack to settle before elective clearance.

modules.name: Chronic Pancreatitis: Drainage, Resection and Pain Surgery

mustKnow.fact: Alcohol and smoking drive most chronic pancreatitis with TIGAR-O risk factors, and Cambridge grades ductal changes from equivocal to marked with chain-of-lakes dilation.
Dilated duct over 7 mm with head mass under 4 cm suits Partington-Rochelle lateral pancreaticojejunostomy, draining the whole duct to relieve pain.
Beger duodenum-preserving head resection cores out the pancreatic head for inflammatory mass with portal hypertension, preserving duodenum and bile duct.
Frey combines head coring with lateral drainage for head mass with dilated duct, giving pain relief matching Whipple with lower morbidity.
Groove or paraduodenal pancreatitis with duodenal wall cysts and Brunner hyperplasia mimics cancer, and pancreaticoduodenectomy is chosen when malignancy cannot be excluded.

Hereditary PRSS1 pancreatitis carries 40 percent lifetime pancreatic cancer risk with surveillance from age 40, and total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplant suits intractable small-duct disease.
Pancreatic ascites and pleural effusion with amylase over 1000 units per L need octreotide with ERCP stenting of the duct disruption, and surgery when leaks persist beyond 3 weeks.
Splenic vein thrombosis with sinistral portal hypertension and gastric varices needs splenectomy, while pseudoaneurysm of the splenic artery over 2 cm needs embolisation.

modules.name: Pancreatic Ductal Cancer: Resectability, Whipple, RAMPS and Adjuvant Therapy

mustKnow.fact: Resectable disease has no arterial contact and venous contact under 180 degrees without contour irregularity, borderline has limited arterial abutment under 180 degrees, and unresectable encases celiac or superior mesenteric artery over 180 degrees.
Pancreaticoduodenectomy removes head, duodenum, distal bile duct and first jejunal loop with Child reconstruction, and pylorus-preserving suits benign and premalignant disease.
RAMPS radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy takes Gerota fascia with N1 nodes for body-tail cancers, improving posterior margin clearance.
Modified FOLFIRINOX for 6 months is the adjuvant standard after resection per PRODIGE 24, and neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX converts borderline disease with CA 19-9 response guiding resection.
Postoperative pancreatic fistula is drain amylase over 3 times serum from day 3, graded ISGPS A biochemical through C with organ failure, managed by drainage, antibiotics and somatostatin analogues.
Delayed gastric emptying needing nasogastric tube beyond day 3 or reinsertion by day 14 is graded ISGPS A to C and managed by prokinetics with pyloric preservation techniques at reoperation.
Germline BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2 testing guides platinum sensitivity and olaparib maintenance per POLO, and all patients get somatic KRAS, mismatch repair and NTRK profiling.
Unresectable head tumours get endoscopic metal biliary stenting with 6 to 10 month patency plus celiac plexus neurolysis for pain, and duodenal obstruction gets enteral stenting or gastrojejunostomy.

modules.name: Pancreatic Cystic Neoplasms: IPMN, MCN, SCN and Surveillance

mustKnow.fact: Branch-duct IPMN under 3 cm without nodules or symptoms enters surveillance with 6-monthly MRI, while main-duct dilation over 10 mm is high-risk stigmata needing resection.
Worrisome features of cyst over 3 cm, thickened enhancing walls, main duct 5 to 9 mm, abrupt calibre change with distal atrophy, lymphadenopathy and CA 19-9 rise need EUS with fine-needle aspiration.
Mucinous cystic neoplasm in middle-aged women with ovarian-type stroma and no duct communication needs resection for all lesions because of malignant potential.
Serous cystadenoma with central scar and spoke-wheel enhancement is benign and observed, resected only for symptoms or diagnostic doubt.
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm in young women with haemorrhagic degeneration needs parenchyma-sparing resection with 95 percent cure because of low-grade behaviour.
Cyst fluid CEA over 192 ng per mL marks mucinous lesions while amylase over 250 units per L marks duct communication, deciding IPMN against MCN.
Post-resection IPMN surveillance continues lifelong with annual imaging because remnant pancreas carries metachronous cancer risk of 5 to 10 percent.
Enucleation suits small benign lesions away from the main duct, but duct proximity under 3 mm risks fistula and favours formal resection.

modules.name: Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumours: Insulinoma, Gastrinoma, MEN1 and Debulking

mustKnow.fact: Grading by Ki-67 under 3 percent for G1, 3 to 20 percent for G2 and over 20 percent for G3 with differentiation decides surgery against systemic therapy.
Insulinoma shows Whipple triad with glucose under 55 mg per dL, insulin over 3 microunits per mL and C-peptide over 0.6 ng per mL during a supervised 72-hour fast.
Gastrinoma triangle spans cystic-cystic duct junction, duodenal sweep and pancreatic neck, with secretin stimulation rise over 120 pg per mL confirming Zollinger-Ellison.
MEN1 with menin mutation needs surveillance from age 5 for parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours, with duodenotomy for multiple duodenal gastrinomas.
Small nonfunctional tumours under 2 cm in the body-tail get enucleation or spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy, while head lesions need Whipple.
Liver metastases get parenchyma-sparing debulking when over 90 percent of disease is resectable, combined with octreotide and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy.
Gallium-68 DOTATATE PET stages somatostatin-avid disease and selects PRRT candidates, while FDG avidity marks aggressive G3 tumours needing chemotherapy.

Glucagonoma with necrolytic migratory erythema, VIPoma with watery diarrhoea and potassium loss, and somatostatinoma with gallstones and diabetes usually sits in the head or duodenum and needs Whipple.

modules.name: Pancreatic and Duodenal Trauma: Ductal Injury and Whipple Decisions

mustKnow.fact: AAST grades pancreatic injury I to V from contusion through distal transection to massive head disruption, with ductal disruption from grade III upward mandating surgery.
Serum amylase is unreliable early, and contrast CT with pancreatic-phase cuts plus MRCP within 24 hours detects ductal injury guiding distal resection against drainage.
Distal transection left of the mesenteric vessels gets spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy when stable, with splenectomy when hilar bleeding or time pressure dominates.
Proximal head injuries with intact ampulla and bile duct get drainage with pyloric exclusion and gastrojejunostomy, while ampullary avulsion or devascularised duodenum needs trauma Whipple.
Duodenal haematoma with high obstruction after blunt trauma in children resolves with 10 to 14 days of nasogastric decompression, confirmed by contrast study before feeding.
Duodenal perforation under 50 percent circumference gets primary transverse closure with omental patch, while over 75 percent or delayed cases need pyloric exclusion with gastrojejunostomy.
Post-traumatic fistula under 200 mL per day closes with octreotide and enteral nutrition in 80 percent, while high-output or persistent leaks beyond 6 weeks need ERCP stenting or resection.
Missed ductal injury presents as pseudocyst or fistula weeks later, managed by internal drainage with cystgastrostomy once the wall matures at 6 weeks.

sections.name: Peritoneum, Hernias, Trauma and Emergency GI Surgery

modules.name: Peritoneal Surface Malignancy: PCI, CRS and HIPEC

mustKnow.fact: Peritoneal cancer index scores 13 abdominopelvic regions 0 to 3 for lesion size, with total over 20 marking extensive disease where complete cytoreduction is unlikely.
Completeness of cytoreduction CC-0 with no visible disease and CC-1 under 2.5 mm decide HIPEC benefit, and CC-2 or CC-3 debulking without HIPEC is avoided.
Pseudomyxoma peritonei from ruptured appendiceal mucinous neoplasm gets complete CRS with mitomycin HIPEC at 42 degrees for 90 minutes, with 10-year survival over 60 percent.
Colorectal peritoneal metastases with PCI under 15 and no extraperitoneal disease get CRS with oxaliplatin or mitomycin HIPEC in trials, while PRODIGE 7 showed no HIPEC add-on benefit.
Diffuse malignant peritoneal mesothelioma with epithelioid histology and BAP1 loss suits CRS with cisplatin HIPEC, while sarcomatoid disease gets systemic therapy.
Gastric peritoneal disease with positive cytology alone gets neoadjuvant FLOT with reassessment, and bulky PCI over 12 is treated palliatively without CRS.
Ovarian peritoneal carcinomatosis gets interval CRS with HIPEC after neoadjuvant chemotherapy per OVHIPEC, with 45.7 month median survival.
Pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy delivers oxaliplatin laparoscopically for unresectable disease, repeated every 6 weeks with PCI reassessment.

modules.name: Small Bowel and Retroperitoneal Tumours: GIST, NET and Desmoid

mustKnow.fact: Small bowel GIST over 5 cm with over 5 mitoses per 5 square mm, over 10 cm at any mitotic rate, or any size with over 10 mitoses or rupture is high risk per modified NIH, needing 3 years of adjuvant imatinib after R0 segmental resection.
Neoadjuvant imatinib for 6 to 12 months shrinks borderline duodenal and rectal GIST to allow organ-preserving surgery, with response judged by Choi density criteria.
Small bowel neuroendocrine tumours with mesenteric desmoplastic mass and flushing-diarrhoea syndrome need bowel resection with mesenteric nodal clearance plus octreotide.
Retroperitoneal sarcoma over 10 cm needs compartmental resection with adjacent organs at specialist centres, with well-differentiated liposarcoma recurring locally and dedifferentiated metastasising.
Desmoid fibromatosis in FAP or after surgery is watched first with 20 percent spontaneous regression, and sorafenib or low-dose chemotherapy suits progressive disease over surgery.
Duodenal adenoma with high-grade dysplasia or ampullary adenoma over 3 cm needs transduodenal ampullectomy or Whipple because of invasive cancer risk.
Peutz-Jeghers small bowel polyps over 1.5 cm get enteroscopic polypectomy to prevent intussusception, with clean sweep laparotomy and intraoperative enteroscopy for heavy burden.

Primary small bowel adenocarcinoma of the duodenum and proximal jejunum presents with obstruction and needs segmental resection with nodal clearance, or Whipple for periampullary growths, with adjuvant capecitabine-oxaliplatin.

modules.name: Inguinal and Femoral Hernia: TEP, TAPP and Chronic Pain

mustKnow.fact: Nyhus types I to IV and EHS lateral-medial-femoral zones with defect size under or over 3 cm standardise reporting and mesh choice for groin hernias.
Lichtenstein tension-free mesh with 6 by 11 cm polypropylene remains the open standard, while TEP avoids peritoneal breach and TAPP aids bilateral and recurrent cases.
Femoral hernia with narrow rigid ring strangulates in 40 percent at presentation, needing McVay Cooper ligament repair or preperitoneal mesh rather than inguinal plug.
Sports hernia with conjoint tendon tear and adductor pain in athletes gets mesh reinforcement after 6 weeks of failed physiotherapy with symphyseal injection.
Chronic post-herniorrhaphy pain over 3 months from ilioinguinal entrapment gets trigger injection first, then laparoscopic triple neurectomy of ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and genitofemoral nerves.
Strangulated groin hernia with bowel compromise gets resection with suture repair in contamination, avoiding synthetic mesh, with staged mesh repair later.
Occult contralateral hernia in 10 percent is repaired at TAPP when found, and watchful waiting suits minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in fit elderly with 1 percent yearly strangulation.
Testicular ischaemia and dysejaculation are consented mesh risks, and lightweight large-pore mesh reduces chronic pain against heavyweight mesh.

modules.name: Ventral and Incisional Hernia: Component Separation and Mesh Planes

mustKnow.fact: EHS widths W1 under 4 cm, W2 4 to 10 cm and W3 over 10 cm with midline or lateral location guide mesh size needing 5 cm overlap beyond the defect.
Retrorectus sublay mesh has the lowest recurrence and infection among planes, while onlay suits small defects and intraperitoneal mesh risks bowel adhesions.
Anterior component separation releases external oblique for 10 cm advancement per side, and transversus abdominis release gives 8 to 12 cm posterior advancement for giant defects.
Botulinum toxin into lateral muscles 6 weeks preoperatively lengthens the abdominal wall and aids closure of defects over 10 cm.
Parastomal hernia in 30 percent of stomas gets Sugarbaker mesh repair or stoma relocation, with prophylactic mesh at index surgery for high-risk patients.
Contaminated defects get staged repair with biologic or biosynthetic mesh, and synthetic mesh is avoided with enteric contamination because infection mandates explantation.
Lumbar and Spigelian hernias through anatomic weak points need preperitoneal mesh because of narrow necks with high strangulation risk.
Smoking cessation 4 weeks and HbA1c under 8 percent precede elective repair, cutting wound infection and recurrence.

modules.name: Acute Abdomen and Peritonitis: Perforation, Damage Control and Open Abdomen

mustKnow.fact: Perforated viscus shows free air under the diaphragm on erect chest film in 70 percent, and CT with oral contrast locates the site with 90 percent accuracy when films are negative.
Mannheim peritonitis index over 26 and APACHE II over 15 predict mortality and intensive care need, guiding damage control against definitive repair.
Damage control laparotomy with abbreviated resection, stapled ends and temporary closure suits unstable acidotic coagulopathic patients, with relook at 24 to 48 hours.
Open abdomen with Bjorck grades 1A clean to 4 frozen abdomen guides temporary closure choice, with negative-pressure therapy and early fascial traction for primary closure.
Colonic perforation with faecal peritonitis gets Hartmann resection, while right-sided perforations with stable physiology suit resection with ileocolic anastomosis.
Typhoid ileal perforation clusters within 60 cm of the valve with multiple antimesenteric ulcers, treated by segmental resection rather than simple closure in endemic zones.
Tuberculous peritonitis with doughy abdomen, ascitic adenosine deaminase over 30 units per L and omental caking needs antitubercular therapy first, with surgery only for obstruction or perforation.
Abdominal tuberculosis strictures get stricturoplasty for short lesions and resection for long or multiple ones after 2 months of antitubercular therapy.

modules.name: Surgical GI Bleeding: Refractory Ulcer, Dieulafoy and Obscure Bleed

mustKnow.fact: Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 allows outpatient care for upper GI bleed, while Rockall over 5 predicts mortality and intensive care need after endoscopy.
Refractory ulcer bleeding after two endoscopic attempts goes to catheter embolisation of the gastroduodenal artery, with surgery reserved for instability or failed embolisation.
Dieulafoy calibre-persistent artery with pinpoint mucosal defect causes massive painless haematemesis, treated by endoscopic clipping with oversewing for failures.
Aortoenteric fistula after aortic graft with herald bleed then exsanguination needs urgent CT angiography and graft excision with extra-anatomic bypass.
Obscure bleeding with negative endoscopy gets capsule endoscopy next, then double-balloon enteroscopy for angioectasia ablation or small bowel tumour resection.
Meckel bleeding in children with painless melena gets technetium scan then segmental resection including the ulcerated ileum opposite the diverticulum.
Lower GI bleed with instability and CT extravasation over 0.5 mL per minute goes to embolisation, while stable diverticular bleeds resolve with 80 percent stopping spontaneously.
Total colectomy is the last resort for unlocalised massive lower bleeding with transfusion over 6 units, after on-table lavage with colonoscopy fails to find the source.

modules.name: Spleen: Trauma, ITP, Cysts and OPSI Prevention

mustKnow.fact: AAST grades splenic injury I to V from capsular tear to shattered spleen, and stable grades I to III without blush get nonoperative care with 90 percent success.
Contrast blush in a stable patient goes to splenic artery embolisation, while instability, hypotension with peritonitis or transfusion over 4 units mandates splenectomy.

Immune thrombocytopenia failing steroids and IVIG with platelets under 30 gets laparoscopic splenectomy with 80 percent durable response, after pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus vaccines 2 weeks prior.
Overwhelming postsplenectomy infection from encapsulated organisms carries 50 percent mortality, prevented by lifelong penicillin in children and early fever antibiotics.

Splenic artery aneurysm over 2 cm, symptomatic or in pregnancy needs embolisation or resection because rupture carries about 25 percent mortality overall, rising toward 70 percent maternal mortality in pregnancy.
Epidermoid splenic cysts over 5 cm with septations need partial splenectomy or decapsulation with omental packing rather than total splenectomy to preserve immunity.
Hereditary spherocytosis with gallstones gets combined splenectomy with cholecystectomy after age 5, with partial splenectomy preferred in children.
Wandering spleen with torsion and infarct on whorled pedicle CT needs splenopexy when viable and splenectomy when infarcted.

modules.name: Short Bowel and Intestinal Failure: Lengthening, Teduglutide and Transplant

mustKnow.fact: Short bowel under 200 cm with colon or under 100 cm without colon causes intestinal failure needing parenteral nutrition with citrulline under 20 micromol per L marking severity.
Ileocecal valve and colon in continuity slow transit and salvage fluids, so jejunocolic anatomy weans faster than end-jejunostomy under 100 cm.
STEP serial transverse enteroplasty staples dilated bowel over 3.5 cm into zigzag channels, lengthening by 50 percent and cutting parenteral need.
Bianchi longitudinal lengthening splits dilated loop along mesenteric leaves for bowel over 4 cm diameter, doubling length while halving calibre.
Teduglutide GLP-2 analogue 0.05 mg per kg daily grows villi and cuts parenteral volume by 20 percent or more in about two thirds of patients (63 percent in STEPS).
Intestinal transplant suits irreversible failure with liver disease, lost venous access or recurrent sepsis, with 5-year survival near 60 percent at expert centres.
D-lactic acidosis with confusion after carbohydrate meals in short bowel needs thiamine, bicarbonate and antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth, not just fluids.
High-output jejunostomy over 2 L per day gets fluid restriction with oral rehydration salts, loperamide, octreotide and proton pump inhibition to cut secretions.

modules.name: Abdominal Trauma: Solid Organs, Hollow Viscus and Retroperitoneum

mustKnow.fact: FAST detects 250 mL of free fluid in Morrison pouch, and positive FAST with instability goes straight to laparotomy while stable positives get CT.
Seat-belt Chance fracture of L1 to L3 with lap-belt ecchymosis predicts hollow viscus and mesenteric injury needing laparotomy despite stable vitals.
Retroperitoneal haematomas from pelvic fracture get binder with angioembolisation, while central zone 1 haematomas from aortic injury need exploration.
Diaphragmatic rupture left side with intrathoracic stomach on chest film needs repair because 30 percent strangulate, and laparoscopy misses 10 percent acutely.
Rectal injury below the peritoneal reflection with faecal soilage gets diversion with presacral drainage, while intraperitoneal rectal wounds get primary repair.
Renal trauma AAST I to III stable gets nonoperative care, grade IV with urinary extravasation gets stenting and grade V with hilar avulsion needs nephrectomy.
Bladder rupture extraperitoneal in 60 percent with pelvic fracture gets catheter drainage for 10 to 14 days, while intraperitoneal rupture needs operative two-layer repair.
Damage control resuscitation with 1 to 1 to 1 red cells, plasma and platelets plus permissive hypotension to systolic 80 to 90 limits coagulopathy before definitive repair.

modules.name: ERAS, Nutrition Access and Anastomotic Leak Management

mustKnow.fact: ERAS pathways with carbohydrate loading 2 hours preoperatively, no bowel prep for colonic cases, thoracic epidural avoidance in laparoscopy and day-1 mobilisation cut stay by 2 to 3 days.
Prehabilitation with 4 weeks of exercise, protein 1.5 g per kg and anaemia correction with intravenous iron reduces complications in frail GI surgery patients.
